entry: Explosive made of [[Nitroglycerin|nitroglycerin]], sorbents such as powdered shells or clay, and stabilizers. Swedish chemist [[Alfred Nobel]] invented it in 1866 and [[Patent|patented]] it the following year. It was the first safely manageable explosive stronger than traditional black powder-based explosives, and it was widely adopted as a safer and more robust alternative. After cement, coal, and sawdust failed, Nobel found that diatomaceous earth stabilized the nitroglycerin into a portable explosive. He tightly controlled the patents, and unlicensed duplicating companies were quickly shut down. He first planned to sell it as "Nobel's Safety Powder" but named it dynamite, from the [[Ancient Greek]] word *dýnamis* (δύναμις), meaning "power." Today it remains in use for controlled blasting in mining and demolition, though it has largely been supplanted by safer alternatives such as [[Ammonium nitrate|ammonium nitrate-based explosives]].

Learning disorder marked by difficulty with [[Arithmetic|arithmetic]], including understanding numbers and performing mathematical calculations. In the United Kingdom it is classified as a specific learning difficulty, and it is sometimes called "math dyslexia." Estimates of its prevalence range from three to six percent of the population. It is associated with dysfunction in the region around the intraparietal sulcus, but it does not reflect a general deficit in cognitive abilities. In 2015, it was established that 11% of children with dyscalculia also have [[Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder|ADHD]].

Type of [[Gastroenteritis|gastroenteritis]] that causes bloody diarrhea, historically known as the bloody flux. It is usually caused by bacteria of the genus *Shigella* (shigellosis) or by the [[Amoeba|amoeba]] *Entamoeba histolytica* (amoebiasis or amoebic dysentery). Other causes may include certain chemicals, other bacteria, other protozoa, and parasitic worms. Risk factors include contamination of food and water with [[Feces|feces]] due to poor [[Sanitation|sanitation]]. Its mechanism involves [[Inflammation|inflammation]] of the intestine, especially the colon. The condition generally resolves within a week, but drinking fluids such as oral rehydration solution is important. [[Antibiotic|Antibiotics]] such as [[Azithromycin]] may be used for cases associated with travel in the developing world. *Shigella* results in about 165 million cases of diarrhea and 1.1 million deaths a year, nearly all in the developing world. Dysentery has been described at least since the time of [[Hippocrates]].

[[Learning disability]] affecting reading, writing, or speaking, also known as word blindness. Difficulties may include spelling, reading quickly, writing words, and pronouncing words aloud, and they are often first noticed at school. Dyslexia is believed to be caused by genetic and environmental factors interacting, and some cases run in families. Dyslexia caused by a [[Stroke|stroke]] or [[Dementia|dementia]] is sometimes called acquired dyslexia. It is the most common learning disability and affects 3–7% of the population in all parts of the world, though up to 20% may have some degree of symptoms. People with dyslexia have higher rates of [[Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder|ADHD]], developmental language disorders, and difficulties with numbers. Treatment adjusts teaching methods and may decrease the impact of symptoms without curing the underlying problem; treatments targeting vision are not effective.

[[Chemical element]] with symbol Dy and atomic number 66. It is a [[Rare-earth element|rare-earth element]] in the [[Lanthanide]] series with a metallic silver luster. It is never found free in nature but occurs in [[Mineral|minerals]] such as xenotime. Natural dysprosium is composed of seven [[Isotope|isotopes]], the most abundant being 164Dy. First identified in 1886 by Paul Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, it was not isolated in pure form until the 1950s. It is used to produce [[Neodymium|neodymium]]-iron-boron (NdFeB) magnets, which are crucial for electric vehicle motors and wind turbines, and for its high thermal neutron absorption cross-section in control rods for [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactors]]. Soluble dysprosium salts are mildly toxic, while insoluble salts are considered non-toxic.

Psychiatric condition known in the DSM-5 as persistent depressive disorder, marked by symptoms similar to those of [[Major depressive disorder]] that last at least two years in adults and one year in children. The term was introduced by Robert Spitzer in the late 1970s as a replacement for the concept of "depressive personality." Symptoms may include fatigue, low self-esteem, poor concentration, and hopelessness, and the condition is frequently comorbid with [[Anxiety disorder|anxiety disorders]], [[Substance use disorder|substance use disorders]], and [[Personality disorder|personality disorders]]. Suicidal ideation is common.

Last nomadic empire of Mongolic Oirat origin, centered on Dzungaria in northern [[Xinjiang]]. Around 1620 the western Mongols known as the Oirats united in the Junggar Basin. In 1678 Galdan received the title Boshogtu Khan from the [[Dalai Lama]], making the Dzungars the leading Oirat tribe. Between 1680 and 1688 they conquered the Tarim Basin and defeated the Khalkha Mongols. In 1696 Galdan was defeated by the [[Qing dynasty]] and lost [[Mongolia|Outer Mongolia]]. The Dzungars conquered [[Tibet]] in 1717 but were driven out in 1720. From 1755 to 1758 the Qing exploited a Dzungar civil war to conquer Dzungaria and wipe out the Dzungar people, which led to Qing conquest of Mongolia and Tibet and the creation of Xinjiang as an administrative unit.

American multinational [[E-commerce|e-commerce]] company based in [[San Jose, California]]. Founded by Pierre Omidyar in September 1995 as AuctionWeb, it lets users buy and sell items through online auctions and "Buy It Now" sales in 190 markets. In 2023 it reported 132 million annual active buyers worldwide and $73 billion in transactions. Its services are accessible through websites and [[Mobile app|mobile apps]]. The company acquired [[PayPal]] in 2002 and spun it off in 2015.

First programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital [[Computer|computer]], completed in 1945. John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert of the [[University of Pennsylvania]] designed it to calculate [[Artillery|artillery]] firing tables for the Ballistic Research Laboratory of the U.S. Army, but its first program was a study of the feasibility of the [[Thermonuclear weapon|thermonuclear weapon]]. It used 17,468 [[Vacuum tube|vacuum tubes]], 7,200 crystal diodes, 1,500 relays, 70,000 resistors, and 10,000 capacitors, and it could perform up to 5,000 additions or subtractions per second. It was programmed with plugboards, switches, and cables rather than stored programs. Its speed was on the order of one thousand times that of electro-mechanical machines. ENIAC was dedicated in February 1946, accepted by the U.S. Army Ordnance Corps in July 1946, and operated at Aberdeen Proving Ground in [[Maryland]] until 1955.

American medical drama television series, 1994–2009. Created by [[Michael Crichton]], it aired on [[NBC]] for 15 seasons and 331 episodes. It is set in the [[Emergency department|emergency room]] of a fictionalized version of Cook County Hospital in [[Chicago]]. It is the second-longest-running primetime medical drama in American television history, behind *Grey's Anatomy*. It won 128 industry awards from 442 nominations, including the Peabody Award and the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Drama Series. As of 2014 it had grossed over $3 billion in television revenue.

American basic cable sports network, founded on September 7, 1979. It is the flagship of ESPN, LLC, a joint venture of [[The Walt Disney Company]] (72%), Hearst Communications (18%), and the [[National Football League]] (10%). It holds extended live rights for the NFL, MLB, NBA, and NHL. As of December 2023, it was available to about 70 million pay television households in the [[United States]], down from a 2011 peak of 100 million. Critics have accused it of biased coverage.

Public research university in [[Zurich]], Switzerland. Founded by the Swiss federal government in 1854, it primarily teaches and conducts research in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Along with its sister institution, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), it forms part of the Swiss Federal Institutes of Technology Domain. In 1911 it received its current name, *Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule*. As of 2025 it enrolled 26,942 students, of whom 4,266 were pursuing doctoral degrees. Students, faculty, and researchers affiliated with it include 22 [[Nobel Prize|Nobel laureates]], among them [[Albert Einstein]], 2 [[Fields Medal|Fields Medalists]], 3 Pritzker Prize winners, and 1 Turing Award recipient. It has 16 departments.

1982 American science fantasy film produced and directed by [[Steven Spielberg]]. It follows Elliott, a boy who befriends an alien stranded on Earth and helps it find its way home. Distributed by [[Universal Pictures]], *E.T.* surpassed *Star Wars* (1977) as the highest-grossing film of all time, a record it held until *Jurassic Park* surpassed it in 1993. It won four Academy Awards from nine nominations, and in 1994 it was selected for the National Film Registry of the [[Library of Congress]].

Commercial activity of buying and selling products and services over the [[Internet]]. It typically uses the [[World Wide Web|web]] for at least part of a transaction, though e-mail and other technologies may also be used. Its three main areas are [[Retail|online retailing]], electronic markets, and online auctions. Typical purchases include books from [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]] and music downloads through digital distribution. Business-to-business (B2B) transactions and direct-to-consumer sales, in which manufacturers sell directly to customers without traditional retail intermediaries, are also significant. Global retail e-commerce sales reached $6.42 trillion in 2025 and are projected to reach $6.88 trillion in 2026. Challenges include consumer data privacy and protection against fraud.

English photographer known for pioneering photographic studies of motion and early motion-picture projection. Born Edward James Muggeridge in Kingston upon Thames, Surrey, he emigrated to the United States at the age of 20 as a bookseller. In the American West he photographed Yosemite Valley, [[San Francisco]], and the newly acquired [[Alaska|Alaskan Territory]]. From 1878 to 1886 he made [[Animal locomotion|chronophotographs of animal locomotion]], using multiple cameras to capture the positions in a stride. His zoopraxiscope projected painted motion pictures from glass discs, predating the flexible film strip used in [[Cinematography|cinematography]]. From 1883 to 1886 he worked at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], producing over 100,000 images of animals and humans in motion. His work influenced [[Thomas Edison]].

Common name for large predatory [[Bird of prey|birds of prey]] in the family Accipitridae. The term has no taxonomic weight, since only the subfamily Aquilinae comprises "true eagles." Most of the 68 species are from [[Eurasia]] and [[Africa]], with two in [[North America]], nine in Central and [[South America]], and three in [[Australia]]. Eagles have heavy beaks, powerful talons, and extremely powerful eyes, and the female of every known species is larger than the male. As [[Apex predator|apex predators]] they hunt sizeable vertebrates, and the extinct [[Haast's eagle]] of New Zealand is recognized as the largest eagle known, estimated at up to 15 kilograms. Eagles usually nest in tall trees or on high cliffs, and many species lay two eggs, though the older chick often kills its younger sibling.

Young open star cluster and [[H II region]] in the [[Constellation|constellation]] Serpens, also cataloged as Messier 16 (M16) or NGC 6611. It was discovered by Jean-Philippe de Cheseaux in 1745–46 and lies in the Sagittarius Arm of the [[Milky Way]], about 5,700 [[Light-year|light-years]] away. The associated cluster contains approximately 8,100 [[Star|stars]]. Images from the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] in 1995 revealed the famous Pillars of Creation, columns of interstellar hydrogen gas and dust that act as incubators for new stars and are sites of active [[Star formation|star formation]]. A 2014 Hubble re-imaging found no evidence of a supernova within the pillars.

American rock band formed in [[Los Angeles]] in 1971. With five number-one singles and six number-one albums, the band sold more than 200 million records worldwide. It was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1998 and has won six [[Grammy Awards]]. *Their Greatest Hits (1971–1975)* is the best-selling album in the United States, with 40 million copies sold. Founding members Glenn Frey, Don Henley, Bernie Leadon, and Randy Meisner had all been recruited by [[Linda Ronstadt]] before forming the band.

Member of the marine mammal family Otariidae, one of three groups of [[Pinniped|pinnipeds]], commonly called [[Sea lion|sea lions]] or fur seals. The family is organized into seven genera and occurs in subpolar, temperate, and equatorial waters of the [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific]], the [[Southern Ocean]], and the southern Indian and Atlantic Oceans. Its name comes from the [[Ancient Greek]] for "little ear," referring to the small but visible external ear flaps that distinguish it from true seals. Otariids have much larger foreflippers than true seals and can turn their hind limbs forward to walk on all fours. They arose in the [[Miocene]] (15–17 million years ago) in the North Pacific. Males are significantly larger than females, and molecular studies no longer support the traditional division into fur seal and sea lion subfamilies.

Family of [[Mammal|mammals]] in the seal lineage Pinnipedia, also called phocids or true seals. They are sometimes called crawling seals to distinguish them from the fur seals and sea lions of Otariidae. Apart from the more tropical monk seals, they are mostly confined to polar, subpolar, and temperate climates, and the Baikal seal is the only exclusively freshwater seal. Adults range from 1.17 m (3.8 ft) and 45 kg (99 lb) in the ringed seal to 5.8 m (19 ft) and 4,000 kg (8,800 lb) in the southern elephant seal, the largest member of the order [[Carnivora]]. Phocids are better long-distance swimmers than otariids but clumsy on land. The earliest known fossil is from [[Italy]], and the family is divided into the subfamilies Phocinae (northern seals) and Monachinae (southern seals).

Series of wars initiated by [[Muhammad]] and continued by the early Muslims, which expanded Muslim rule out of Arabia over the following century. In 622 Muhammad established the first Islamic state in [[Medina]], and armies then expanded under the [[Rashidun Caliphate]] and the [[Umayyad Caliphate]]. At its height, Muslim-ruled territory under the caliphates is estimated to have covered 13,000,000 square kilometers (5,000,000 sq mi), from the Indian subcontinent to the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. The conquests overran the [[Sasanian Empire]] and confined the [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantines]] to part of Anatolia and southeastern Europe. Most historians cite the exhaustion of both empires after decades of mutual warfare, further accelerated by the Sasanian civil war of 628–632, as a key factor in the Muslim success.

Branch of education theory concerned with teaching children from birth to age eight. The field emerged during the Enlightenment in European countries with high literacy rates and grew through the 19th century as [[Primary education|universal primary education]] became the norm. It is a prevalent public policy issue, with debate over developmentally appropriate play versus academic preparation in [[Reading|reading]], writing, and math. As of 2023, "only around 4 in 10 children aged 3 and 4 attend early childhood education" worldwide. Participation is around 2 in 3 children in Latin America and the Caribbean, compared with only 1 in 4 in [[Sub-Saharan Africa]]. The [[OECD]] describes high-quality early childhood education and care as a cost-effective way to enhance children's cognitive, social, and emotional development. The Developmental Interaction Approach draws on the theories of Jean Piaget, [[Erik Erikson]], and [[John Dewey]].

Spread of [[Human|humans]] from Africa across the world. Early expansions of [[Homo erectus]] out of Africa began about 2 million years ago, reaching Eurasia around 1.8 million years ago and Southeast Asia, including [[Java]], about 1.7 million years ago. *Homo sapiens* dispersed from East Africa roughly 70–50,000 years ago, spreading along the southern coast of Asia to Oceania by about 50,000 years ago and across Europe about 40,000 years ago. *H. heidelbergensis*, which lived around 500,000 years ago, was the likely ancestor of [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]], [[Denisovan|Denisovans]], and modern humans. After the [[Last Glacial Maximum]], North Eurasian populations migrated to the Americas about 20,000 years ago. [[Polynesia]] was reached within the past 2,000 years in the last wave of the Austronesian expansion.

Term for *Homo sapiens* whose anatomy matches that of contemporary humans, distinguishing them from extinct archaic humans. The earliest fossil evidence appears in [[Africa]] around 300,000 years ago. The [[Skull|Florisbad Skull]] in [[South Africa]], dated to about 259,000 years ago, and remains from [[Ethiopia]] dated to about 233,000 to 196,000 years ago are among the oldest known. Early modern humans interbred with [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]] and [[Denisovan|Denisovans]], incorporating 1–2% Neanderthal DNA into non-African genomes. Linnaeus coined the binomial name in 1758.

Outermost shell of [[Rock (geology)|rock]], comprising less than one percent of Earth's radius and volume. It is the top component of the [[Lithosphere]], which is broken into [[Plate tectonics|tectonic plates]] and lies on the denser mantle. Temperature rises with depth, by as much as 30 °C (54 °F) per kilometer in the upper crust. Continental crust is 25–70 km (about 15–44 mi) thick and composed of less dense, more felsic rocks such as [[Granite]]. Oceanic crust is 5–10 km thick and composed primarily of denser, more mafic rocks such as [[Basalt]]. The most abundant minerals in continental crust are [[Feldspar]], about 41% by mass, followed by [[Quartz]] at 12% and [[Pyroxene]] at 11%.
